chunks: UART device count and direction. The question: How many devices can talk to each other? What is the direction of communication?
A basic UART link joins exactly two devices. Each wire has one sender and one receiver.
Because TX and RX are separate wires, both devices can talk at the same moment, which is called full duplex.
If you want a third device, you cannot just join its TX onto an existing wire.
To reach more devices you add more UARTs, use a shared bus standard such as RS-485 with addresses, or pick a different bus like I2C.
Picture a phone call where each person has their own line, one for speaking and one for listening. Both can talk at once, and nothing collides.
Now a third person wants to join by speaking into the same line as someone else. Two voices on one line become a muddle.
A group needs a meeting with a chair, where only one person speaks at a time and each is called by name.
Two wires, each with exactly one driver and one receiver. The two directions are independent, so A and B can transmit simultaneously (full duplex).
Point-to-point: a link between exactly two endpoints. Full duplex: both directions at the same time, because each direction has its own wire.
Contention: two outputs driving opposite levels onto one wire at once. RS-485: a shared two-wire bus standard whose drivers can switch off, so many devices can take turns.
Addressing: a rule in the message, such as a device number, that says who should answer.
Take two chips on a 3. 3 volts board. A's TX goes to B's RX, and B's TX goes to A's RX. Now suppose you tie two TX pins together, and one drives high while the other drives low.
If each output switch has about 25 ohms, current flows through both: 3. 3 over (25 plus 25) equals 66 milliamps. The wire sits near 1. 65 volts, which is neither a one nor a zero.
That is the whole idea.
"Basic UART is point to point: two devices, each wire with one driver. TX of one goes to RX of the other, and vice versa, so both directions work at once, which is full duplex.
You can't just wire more TX pins together because push-pull drivers would fight.
To reach more devices, use one UART each, or RS-485 with tri-state drivers and an addressing protocol like Modbus, which is half duplex, or the 9-bit address mode.
For many devices, I'd move to I2C or SPI."
